method_card.title: Histograms and Frequency Density
method_card.content:
A histogram with unequal class widths uses frequency density on the y-axis, not frequency. This is a Higher-tier only skill.

Important: the formula \(\text{frequency density} = \frac{\text{frequency}}{\text{class width}}\) is NOT given on the formula sheet — you must recall it.

The reason for using frequency density is that the area of each bar represents the frequency, not the height. If you plotted frequency on the y-axis with unequal class widths, wider classes would appear taller even with the same or fewer items, misleading the reader.

The two core directions you need to master are:

  • Forward (frequency → density): calculate the class width, then divide the frequency by the class width to get the bar height.
  • Reverse (density → frequency): multiply the bar height (frequency density) by the class width to get back to the frequency. This is the more commonly tested direction.

When reading a histogram, multiply each bar’s height by its class width to recover the frequency. To find the total number of items, sum all recovered frequencies. To estimate a proportion or probability, sum the relevant frequencies and divide by the total.

Recognising misrepresentation: if someone draws a histogram with unequal class widths but uses frequency (not frequency density) on the y-axis, the wider bars are misleadingly tall. This is specifically listed in the specification as a misrepresentation error to recognise.
steps: Recall the formula: frequency density = frequency ÷ class width
Calculate each class width from the interval boundaries
For forward problems: divide frequency by class width to get bar height
For reverse problems: multiply bar height by class width to get frequency
Sum all recovered frequencies to find the total
Check by confirming total area = total frequency

exam_context.marks: 3–6 marks; forward and reverse calculations are typically 1 mark each; full histogram problems combining both directions are 4–6 marks
exam_context.frequency: Appears on most Higher tier papers; the reverse calculation (density × width = frequency) is tested more often than the forward direction

worked_examples.question: A class interval 20–30 has frequency 15. Calculate the frequency density for this bar.
A histogram bar for the class 40–60 has a frequency density of 3.5. What is the frequency for this class?
A histogram shows four bars. Class 0–10: height 2.4; Class 10–20: height 3.8; Class 20–40: height 1.9; Class 40–70: height 0.6. Find the total frequency represented by the histogram.

steps.label: Step 1 — Find each frequency using frequency = height × class width

bronze.display: A class interval 0–5 has frequency 20. What is the frequency density?

misconceptions.message: Frequency density = frequency ÷ class width = 20 ÷ 5 = 4. Do not use frequency as the bar height.

bronze.display: A class interval 10–30 has frequency 40. What is the frequency density?

misconceptions.message: Class width = 30 − 10 = 20. Frequency density = 40 ÷ 20 = 2.

bronze.display: A histogram bar for class 5–15 has height (frequency density) = 3. What is the frequency?

misconceptions.message: Frequency = frequency density × class width = 3 × 10 = 30. The bar height is NOT the frequency.

bronze.display: A histogram bar for class 20–50 has frequency density 1.6. What is the frequency?

misconceptions.message: Class width = 50 − 20 = 30. Frequency = 1.6 × 30 = 48.

bronze.display: Which formula correctly gives the frequency density for a histogram bar?
options: Frequency × class width
Frequency ÷ class width
Class width ÷ frequency
Frequency + class width

misconceptions.message: Frequency density = frequency ÷ class width. This formula is NOT on the formula sheet — you must recall it.

bronze.display: A class 0–20 has frequency 36. A class 20–30 has frequency 24. Which class has the greater frequency density?
options: Class 0–20 (width 20)
Class 20–30 (width 10)
Both have the same frequency density
Cannot tell without the histogram

misconceptions.message: Class 0–20: density = 36/20 = 1.8. Class 20–30: density = 24/10 = 2.4. Class 20–30 has the greater frequency density despite having fewer items.

bronze.display: A bar in a histogram for class 0–4 has frequency density 5. What is the frequency for this class?

misconceptions.message: Frequency = 5 × 4 = 20. Class width = 4 − 0 = 4.

bronze.display: A histogram bar for class 100–200 has height 0.8 (frequency density). What is the frequency?

misconceptions.message: Class width = 200 − 100 = 100. Frequency = 0.8 × 100 = 80.

silver.display: A frequency table has four classes with these frequencies: 0–10: 25; 10–20: 40; 20–40: 30; 40–80: 20. Calculate the frequency density for the class 20–40.

misconceptions.message: Class width = 40 − 20 = 20. Frequency density = 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5.

silver.display: A histogram shows two bars. Class 0–10 has height 4.5 and class 10–30 has height 2.2. What is the combined frequency of both classes?
A histogram bar for class 0–5 has frequency density 6. The bar for class 5–15 has frequency density 3. What is the total frequency across both classes?
A histogram has class 0–20 with frequency density 2.5 and class 20–25 with frequency density 8. Which class has the greater frequency?
options: Class 0–20 (frequency 50)
Class 20–25 (frequency 40)
Both classes have the same frequency
Class 20–25 (frequency 8)

misconceptions.message: Class 0–20: 2.5 × 20 = 50. Class 20–25: 8 × 5 = 40. Class 0–20 has the greater frequency despite its lower bar height.

silver.display: A frequency table: class 0–10 has frequency 35, class 10–20 has frequency 35, class 20–50 has frequency 42. What is the frequency density for class 20–50?

misconceptions.message: Class width = 50 − 20 = 30. Frequency density = 42 ÷ 30 = 1.4.

silver.display: A histogram shows bars for three classes. Class A (0–5): height 3.2; Class B (5–10): height 4.0; Class C (10–20): height 1.8. What percentage of the total is in Class B?

misconceptions.message: Class A: 3.2×5=16. Class B: 4.0×5=20. Class C: 1.8×10=18. Total=54. % in B = (20/54)×100 = 37.0%. Re-check: 20/54 ≈ 37.0, not 40. Use exact calculation.

gold.display: A histogram has four bars with the following details. Class 0–10: frequency density 1.8. Class 10–25: frequency density 3.2. Class 25–40: frequency density 2.4. Class 40–60: frequency density 0.9. What is the total frequency?
A histogram shows class 10–20 with frequency density 4.5 and class 20–30 with frequency density 3.5. A student claims both bars represent the same frequency. Are they correct?
options: Yes — both bars have equal class widths so frequency = density for both
No — class 10–20 has frequency 45 and class 20–30 has frequency 35
Yes — the same frequency density means the same frequency
No — you need more information to determine the frequencies

misconceptions.message: Both class widths = 10. Class 10–20: 4.5 × 10 = 45. Class 20–30: 3.5 × 10 = 35. Same width means the one with higher density has higher frequency.

gold.display: A histogram shows three classes. Class 0–10: height 2.0; Class 10–20: height 5.0; Class 20–50: height 1.0. Estimate the number of values in the range 15–30.

misconceptions.message: 15–20 is the upper half of the class 10–20 (width 5): 5.0 × 5 = 25. 20–30 is the first third of class 20–50 (width 10 out of 30): 1.0 × 10 = 10. Total = 25 + 10 = 35. This assumes uniform distribution within classes.

gold.display: A histogram has a bar for class 0–20 with frequency density 3.5 and a bar for class 20–30 with height h. The frequency in class 20–30 is twice the frequency in class 0–20. Find h.

misconceptions.message: Class 0–20 frequency = 3.5 × 20 = 70. Class 20–30 frequency = 2 × 70 = 140. Class width = 10. h = 140 ÷ 10 = 14.

gold.display: A histogram is drawn for a dataset with classes 0–5, 5–10, 10–20, 20–40 using frequency on the y-axis instead of frequency density. The class 10–20 has frequency 30 and the class 20–40 has frequency 30. A student looks at the bars and says 'both classes have the same number of values'. Explain the error in the histogram.
options: There is no error — equal frequencies always produce equal bar heights
The y-axis should show frequency density; the 20–40 bar should be half the height of the 10–20 bar because its class is twice as wide
The 20–40 bar should be twice the height because its class is wider
Frequencies should always be shown on the y-axis for accuracy

misconceptions.message: With unequal widths, using frequency on the y-axis misleads: the 20–40 bar (width 20) appears as tall as the 10–20 bar (width 10) despite covering twice the range. Frequency density corrects this — class 10–20 density = 30/10 = 3, class 20–40 density = 30/20 = 1.5, so the wider bar is correctly half the height.

gold.display: A histogram shows four classes. Class 0–10: fd = 1.5; Class 10–15: fd = 6.0; Class 15–20: fd = 4.0; Class 20–40: fd = 0.75. What fraction of all values are in the class 10–15? Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.
